paper.title: International trade and retail market performance and structure: Theory and empirical evidence
paper.code_data_availability: Acknowledgements (p. 112): 'The data builds on anonymized micro data sets owned by Statistics Denmark (SD). …

registers.years: 1999-2008 (1997 and 1998 also used for the lag structure)
registers.role: sample frame and outcomes: industry affiliation, employees, turnover, value added, profits, fixed and total assets, firm resignation date (exit)
treatment: firm-level export and import activity at detailed product level and by partner country (Intrastat for intra-EU, Extrastat for extra-EU trade)
variables_mentioned: import values by HS product code and partner country

registers.role: shop (branch) level information: location and individuals working there; used to count shops per retail firm, define local retail markets and compute Herfindahl indices
variables_mentioned: number of employees and wage bill at the shop level

linkages: firms merged across FIRM, UHDI and IDAS through a unique firm identifier
shops linked to their retail firm in IDAS to count shops per firm and to identify chains
firm-level sales and assets distributed across a chain's shops using each shop's share of the firm's total employment, then aggregated to region x sector local retail markets

sample.universe: Danish firms reporting retailing as their main activity, in the 24 retained six-digit retail industries, present in Denmark between 1999 and 2008
sample.unit_of_observation: firm-year for the firm-level analyses; local retail market (region x sector) by year for the market-level analysis
selection_rules: all firms whose main activity reported in FIRM is retailing (six-digit industry level)
drop NACE rev. 1 three-digit industries 522, 523, 525, 526 and 527; 24 retail industries retained

drop observations with implausible values for key variables (e.g. negative sales) and outliers deviating from the median by more than five times the standard deviation of the labour productivity distribution; clean dependent variables by dropping year-on-year growth rates deviating by more than five standard deviations from the median
controlling for the log of the number of employees restricts the analysis to firms with at least one employee
profit and markup regressions use only firms with strictly positive profits / an estimated markup (around 9% of firms report zero or negative profits)
market-level analysis: only firms that can be merged to IDAS; NACE four-digit industries 5211 and 5212 excluded for 1999-2001
matching analyses: import starters (no imports in t-2 and t-1, imports in t) versus firms not importing in any of the three years, on common support
sample.n_observations: 92,021 firm-years in the baseline sales regression; 119,058 firm-years in the exit regressions; 13,735 market-years in the Herfindahl regressions

construction_notes: firm-level domestic sales, value added and wages deflated by the consumer price index with 2000 as the base year
markups estimated following De Loecker and Warzynski (2012); details in the Online Appendix
consumer goods defined on the BEC classification (BEC codes 112, 122, 522, 61, 62, 63), merged to HS six-digit product codes
imports measured as direct imports from markets outside the EU15
a chain is a firm with at least two shops
85 regions formed to concord Danish municipality codes across the 2007 municipality reform; a local retail market is a region x sector cell
shops of the same firm in a given region and industry treated as a single shop when computing the Herfindahl index
DSIZE marks firms in the lower 25th percentile of the total-assets size distribution; LN(VIMPst) is mean-centered in the exit regressions

links.pointer_quote: Using Danish microdata for the period 1999 to 2008, we find that sales, profits, and markups of importing retailers exceed those of domestically sourcing firms on average by 20%, 27%, and 3%, respectively, after controlling for firm characteristics.

claims.statement: Danish retail firms that directly import consumer goods from outside the EU15 have higher sales than non-importing retailers in the same sector and year, conditional on lagged firm size

register_source.value: UHDI (udenrigshandel diskretioneret): firm-level import values by product and partner country (Intrastat and Extrastat)

definition.value: Dummy equal to one if firm i imports consumer goods from at least one non-EU15 market in year t, and zero for firms not importing from these markets; the comparison group comprises firms that source domestically only and those that also source from EU15 markets. Consumer goods are defined on the BEC classification merged to HS six-digit product codes.

timing.value: year t, contemporaneous with the outcome

outcome.label: Log of Sales (LN(SALES)): log firm-level domestic sales

register_source.value: FIRM (generel firmastatistik): turnover / domestic sales

definition.value: Logarithm of firm-level domestic sales taken from FIRM, deflated by the consumer price index with 2000 as the base year.

timing.value: year t, the same year as the import status dummy

units.value: log points of the dependent variable (coefficient on a 0/1 dummy; the dependent variable is log transformed, so the paper converts coefficients as (exp(b)-1)*100 percent)

magnitude.interpretation: the sales, profits, and markups of directly importing firms exceed those of their non-importing counterparts on average by 20%, 27%, and 3% (columns i to iii); footnote 45 converts e.g. 0.18 into 19.7 = (exp(0.18)-1)*100

estimand.target_population: Danish retail firms with at least one employee in the 24 retained retail industries, 1999-2008
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: import status and outcome measured in the same year t

population.description: Danish retail firms (main activity retailing) with at least one employee in the 24 retained six-digit retail industries, 1999-2008
population.selection: firms whose main activity reported in FIRM is retailing, in 24 retained retail industries; at least one employee (implied by controlling for log employees); implausible values and labour-productivity outliers dropped

identification.source_of_variation: cross-firm (and, with firm fixed effects, within-firm) variation in direct import status of Danish retailers, 1999-2008; the authors assume the observed increase in import activity is at least in part driven by a trade cost reduction

key_assumptions.assumption: The import premium regressions compare importing and non-importing firms within sector-year pairs, conditional on lagged firm size; the authors state that these regressions provide no indication of causality.

threats_discussed: the estimates cannot distinguish self-selection of larger, higher markup and more profitable retailers into importing (Hypothesis 2) from performance effects caused by import activity (Hypothesis 3)
off-the-shelf instruments for firm-level imports available from the literature turned out to perform unconvincingly / to be rather weak
robustness_checks: specifications estimated with and without firm fixed effects
propensity score matching estimates of the same relationships (Tables 6 and 9)
unresolved_confounders: self-selection of larger, higher markup and therefore more profitable retailers into importing: the authors state these regressions provide no indication of causality

estimation.specification: Eq. (14): log outcome on DIMPit, LN(EMPLOYEESit-1) and sector-year dummies
controls: LN(EMPLOYEESit-1): log number of employees, lagged

value.lhs: yrst (market-level Herfindahl index, in logs)
value.parameter_of_interest: b1
value.normalisation: local market (region x sector) fixed effects and year dummies absorb level differences, so b1 is identified from within-market variation; both dependent and independent variable are in logs, so b1 is an elasticity

value.claimed_domain: other industrialized / advanced economies whose consumer goods trade and retailing developments mirror Denmark's
boundary_conditions: Danish retailing is subject to a zoning regulation limiting maximum shop size; the authors note that regulation may limit how far large, productive retailers can adjust to trade, and that countries without such regulation may have experienced bigger retail market adjustments

theory_referenced: partial equilibrium model of a retail industry with heterogeneous firms and endogenous shop margin, extending Raff and Schmitt (2012) and Basker and Van (2010a)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Like Basker and Van, we find a significant correlation between imports and retail market concentration.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: effects of a trade cost reduction on average retail productivity and markups (Hypothesis 5), on the number of shops in a local market (Hypothesis 6), and on the mean and variance of shop-level sales (Hypothesis 7) -- stated to be in the Online Appendix only
